title: Fewest Squares That Sum to N
statement: A square number is k × k for some whole k ≥ 1: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 and so on. Given a positive integer n, return the smallest count of square numbers that add up to exactly n. The same square may be used more than once.

examples.why: 9 + 9. Taking the biggest square first gives 16 + 1 + 1, which uses 3.

hints: Grabbing the largest square that fits does not always work. Look at 18.
Let best[i] be the answer for i. The last square used is some j × j ≤ i. What is left over?
best[i] = 1 + min over j of best[i − j²]. Fill it from 1 up to n; it costs O(n√n).

explain.intuition:
Greedy fails: for 18 the biggest square, 16, leaves 2 = 1 + 1, so three squares, while 9 + 9 needs only two. You have to consider every possible last square.

If the last square in the best sum for i is j², the rest is the best sum for i − j². So best[i] = 1 + min(best[i − j²]) over all j with j² ≤ i. There are about √i choices for each i, which gives O(n√n) work in total. It is the same shape as making change with the fewest coins, where the coins are the squares.
steps: Create best of size n + 1 with best[0] = 0 and the rest set to infinity.
For each i from 1 to n, try every j with j × j ≤ i.
pitfalls: Taking the largest square that fits. 18 and 32 both break it.
Starting j at 0. Then 0 counts as a square and the loop never improves anything.
Assuming the answer is at most 3. Numbers like 7 and 28 need four squares.

solutions.title: Bottom-up DP over the last square
solutions.idea: best[i] is one more than the best answer for i minus some square. Fill the table in increasing order.

solutions.title: BFS over remainders
solutions.idea: Each level of a BFS subtracts one more square. The first level that reaches 0 is the answer, and a visited set stops repeats.

solutions.title: Number theory shortcut
solutions.idea: Every number is a sum of at most four squares, and exactly four are needed when n has the form 4^a(8b + 7). Otherwise test 1 and 2 directly; anything else is 3.

followups: Return one shortest list of squares, not just the count.
Why does BFS usually finish much faster than the DP here, even though both are O(n√n) in the worst case?
